name: Chloe Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at the Red Hill copper pit, one of the big ones, about 240 tonnes loaded. Day shift starts at six with the pre-start check, walking round the truck with a torch, then I'm on the ramp hauling ore from the shovel to the crusher for twelve hours. I'm the crew lead on my panel, so I also sort out who's on which truck and I'm the one the young drivers radio when something feels off. I like the rhythm of it and I like my crew, but the night rotation wears me out more every year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Seventeen years at Red Hill. I started on a water cart when my eldest wasn't even thought of, and I've been the shop steward for our crew for six of those years. My partner Marco drives a school bus, so between us we know every pothole in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Every year there's a new gadget the company says will change everything, and mostly it's another screen in the cab that beeps at you. I'd say it at the crib table and I'd say it at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it'd be a relief. I don't use any of that AI stuff, I don't want to, and if it stays a toy in the office then my job looks like my job for the next twenty years. I could stop reading the headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. I'd keep driving, keep putting the usual bit into savings, and keep pushing the company on the roster because the fatigue is the real problem on my crew, not robots. I'd probably finally book the camping trip we keep cancelling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit smug maybe. Like the weather forecast said storm and it just rained a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the fatigue is the real problem. What does that look like on a bad night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four in the morning, coming down the ramp with a full load, you can feel your eyes going heavy. Two years ago a lad on B crew clipped a berm because he nodded off for a second. Nobody was hurt, but that's what I lose sleep over, not some computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about this picture still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the company would still try it. Hype or not, they'd trial something on our trucks just to say they did. I'd want the union in the room for that trial, not told about it afterwards.

S0.say: I'd tell the crib table and the union meeting that I called it, because the company sells a new miracle gadget every year and it always ends up as another beeping screen in the cab.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved that my job stays my job for the next twenty years. I don't use AI and don't want to, so I could finally stop reading the scary headlines.
S0.do: Keeps driving and keeps her usual savings going. Pushes the company on the night roster and fatigue instead, and plans the family camping trip that keeps getting cancelled.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, like a storm warning that turned into light rain.
S0.quote: About four in the morning, coming down the ramp with a full load, you can feel your eyes going heavy.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe's real worry in a quiet world is fatigue on the night shift, and she turned the question there straight away. Even when nothing changes she wants the union present at any trial, which shows how her steward role frames everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has to bring the workers along, not just bring the trucks in. Out loud I'd be the one saying there has to be a deal: retraining paid for, no forced redundancies, people moved into new roles before anyone is let go. I'd post that on the union page too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think haul trucks are the first thing they'd go for. Driverless trucks already run at other big pits, everybody knows that, and our trucks drive the same loop a thousand times. If any job at Red Hill shrinks, it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to open talks the first month, before the trucks show up, and I'd want it in writing how many drivers they keep. At home we'd stop the kitchen extension we've been saving for and leave that money sitting, about four months of bills. I'm not going to go learning computers at 43, I'd fight for the jobs we've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like hearing a noise in the engine and knowing you can keep driving for now but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some drivers might move into new roles, like watching the trucks from a control room. Would you go for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've seen that control room at the other site on a union visit, people sitting at six screens in a dark room. I'd last a week. I'd rather they kept some of us in cabs for the odd jobs, the wet weather and the tight spots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be worried about on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tanya, she's 26, single mum, been driving two years. She's quick but she's got no seniority, and when they cut, it goes last in, first out. I'd be fighting for her as much as for me.

S1.say: I'd say out loud, and on the union page, that the company has to bring the workers along with the trucks. That means paid retraining, no forced redundancies and new roles lined up before anyone is let go.
S1.think: I think haul trucks are first on the list because driverless ones already run at other big pits. If any job at Red Hill shrinks, it's mine, and I'm not sure the union can stop it.
S1.do: Gets the union to open talks in the first month and demands written driver numbers. Freezes the kitchen extension and keeps about four months of bills in savings, but turns down retraining for a control room job.
S1.feel: Anxious and braced, like an engine noise she can drive on for now but not forever.
S1.quote: People sitting at six screens in a dark room. I'd last a week.
S1.fieldNote: She knows exactly how exposed haul driving is and says so plainly in private. Her answer is to fight through the union rather than adapt herself, and she won't consider the control room path. Her concern for a younger driver on her crew came up without prompting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say this is the biggest theft of work there's ever been and the government has to step in, tax the companies running these robots and pay people while they work out what's next. I'd be at every meeting and every rally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'd be out within the year. Two years isn't enough for anything, not for the union, not for me. The company would have driverless trucks on the ramp the minute they could buy them, and four months of savings is four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week I'd sit down with Marco and go through every bill. The car loan goes, the kids' swimming goes, we'd look at renting out the spare room. I'd push the union for the biggest payout we can get and I'd sign up for whatever campaign wants a public income for people like us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor has dropped and I'm still standing on air.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years of warning, what's the first thing you'd try to do before the change actually lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the payout terms locked in before they need us less. Right now they still need drivers, so that's when you've got something to bargain with. Once the trucks are running themselves, nobody's going to listen to a steward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's eleven, she'd ask straight out. I'd tell her Mum's job is changing and we're going to be okay because we stick together. I'm not sure I'd believe it while I said it.

S2.say: I'd say this is the biggest theft of work ever and the government has to step in. They should tax the companies running the robots and pay people while they work out what comes next.
S2.think: I think I'd be out within the year, because two years isn't enough for anyone to prepare. Four months of savings only lasts four months.
S2.do: Goes through every bill with Marco in the first week and cuts the car loan and the kids' swimming. Pushes the union to lock in payouts while drivers are still needed and joins the campaign for a public income.
S2.feel: Sick and shaken, like the floor has dropped away under her.
S2.quote: Right now they still need drivers, so that's when you've got something to bargain with.
S2.fieldNote: With only two years, Chloe shifts from saving jobs to bargaining for exits while drivers still have bargaining power. She blames the companies and looks to government and the union, not to herself. She admitted she wouldn't believe her own reassurance to her daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but I'd say we've got a window and we need to use it. Five years is time to get laws written, to make the companies share what they save. I'd be telling everyone at the pit to join the union now, not when it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means I'd still lose the truck, just not tomorrow. Five years gets me to 48, and that's a horrible age to start again. But at least the kids would be through most of school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years building up savings, pushing it from four months to maybe eight, and paying the mortgage down a bit. I'd stand for the regional union committee, because that's where the deals get done. I still wouldn't retrain into screens, but I might look at the water treatment plant on site, because somebody has to fix things when they break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but I can breathe. Five years feels like a long ramp instead of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you won't retrain, but now you're looking at the water plant. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I suppose I mean I won't go and sit in front of a computer all day. Fixing pumps is still real work with your hands, and I know some of the fitters. That I could stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between grabbing a payout and actually getting a deal. With two years you're just trying to get out with something. With five you can get the law changed before the trucks arrive, and that's what I'd want.

S3.say: I'd say we've got a window and must use it to get laws written so the companies share what they save. I'd tell everyone at the pit to join the union now, not when it's too late.
S3.think: I'd still lose the truck, just not tomorrow, and 48 is a horrible age to start again. At least the kids would be through most of school by then.
S3.do: Builds savings from about four to eight months and pays down some mortgage over two years. Stands for the regional union committee and looks at a hands-on job at the mine's water treatment plant.
S3.feel: Still anxious, but able to breathe, like a long ramp instead of a cliff.
S3.quote: It's the difference between grabbing a payout and actually getting a deal.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turns Chloe from damage control to campaigning for laws. When I pointed out she'd ruled out retraining, she softened and drew her line at screen work, not at learning something new. Hands-on work is the line for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse. If the government and the companies let people fall through the cracks with a whole decade's notice, that's a choice they made. I'd keep saying that till they're sick of hearing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years puts me at 53. Part of me thinks I could just keep driving until the trucks are gone and then go. But I know that's the kind of thinking that catches people out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep the union work going, that's the main thing. I'd put a bit extra into savings every month and pay the mortgage down harder, so it's nearly gone by the time it hits. I'd want both kids pointed at trades the robots can't easily do, or at university if they want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit tired. It's a long time to carry a worry around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said that's the kind of thinking that catches people out. Have you seen it happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle was at the old lead mine when it closed. They'd heard rumours for years and he kept saying they'd never shut it. He was 55 and never really worked again, just odd jobs and the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So with ten years, what would you do differently from your uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have the house paid off, mostly. And not pretend. I'd still hate the idea of a screen job, but I'd have something lined up on site with my hands, even if it's the water plant or the tyre bay.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse. If people fall through the cracks with a decade's notice, the government and the companies chose that.
S4.think: Part of me thinks I could drive until the trucks are gone at 53 and then go. I know that's exactly the thinking that caught my uncle out when the lead mine shut.
S4.do: Keeps driving and keeps up the union work. Puts extra into savings and the mortgage each month so the house is nearly paid off, and lines up a hands-on job on site for later.
S4.feel: Uneasy and tired of carrying a long worry.
S4.quote: He was 55 and never really worked again, just odd jobs and the pub.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Chloe relax into her routine, and she caught herself doing it, citing her uncle's lost years after the lead mine closed. Her plan is mostly financial and political rather than personal retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. That's the one where you don't even get to fight, you just watch it happen. What would help is a law that says if a company replaces you with a machine, they keep paying into a fund that pays you while you find something else, and that the union gets a say before the first truck arrives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame. I'd blame the people who'll make the money, not the engineers and not the robots. A truck doesn't decide to sack anybody, a board does.

headlineQuote: A truck doesn't decide to sack anybody, a board does.
portrait: Chloe Santos is a 43-year-old haul truck driver and crew lead at the Red Hill copper pit, a union steward with a school bus driver partner, two kids and a mortgage. She never uses AI and has no wish to retrain into control room work, which she says she'd last a week in. Across the scenarios she reaches for the union and for laws first, from demanding a seat at any trial to campaigning for a fund paid by companies that automate. Her mood rises from calm to alarmed as the timeline shortens, and longer warning mostly gives her time to pay down the house and line up hands-on work on site.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there'd be no time to fight and she'd just watch drivers get replaced.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies that replace workers with machines pay into a fund that supports them while they find new work, and a union say before any driverless truck arrives.
